articles.title: The Tehran opening
articles.content: HELD amid the threat of a renewed US-Israeli attack on Iran and escalating conflict in the Arabian Peninsula, themeetingbetween Iranian leaders and members of the Makkah Defence Alliance was deeply significant — though it remained unclear whether the talks had produced any major breakthrough. The quadrilateral meeting reportedly discussed “regional cooperation, the US-Israeli aggression against Iran and its consequences”, among other topics. It was the first high-level contact between Iran and all of the alliance’s members since Saudi Arabia was drawn deeper into its conflict with the Houthis. The gathering came days after a brief visit to Tehran by Pakistan’s army chief, during which he reportedly proposed the meeting — a suggestion Iranian leaders responded to positively. That visit was essentially a part of Pakistan’s mediatory efforts to restart the stalled peace talks between America and Iran, and a response to the latest flare-up in the region. Since the collapse of a briefceasefirereached in April, the United States has imposed an economic blockade on Iran in an attempt to force it to capitulate. It has not. Iran has kept control of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas used to flow. The diplomatic efforts of Pakistan and Qatar have so far failed to break the stalemate. The main stumbling block to resuming peace talks has been President Trump’s insistence that Iran give up its enriched uranium stockpile. Iran has refused, insisting that the US must end its naval blockade and start negotiations on the seven points that overlap with the Islamabad memorandum of understanding. Iranian leaders have repeatedly declared that “not a single particle of enriched nuclear material” would leave Iran. Regional peace can be ensured only through a regional security architecture. Tensions rose further withreportsof a possible joint US-Israeli attack on Iran before the US midterm elections. According to American media, Israel had been pressing Trump to resume airstrikes before Israel’s own general elections, which were held yesterday. There are still indications that Trump could restart military action after the American midterms on Nov 3. Iranian officials warned last week that if Iran were attacked again, its forces would widen their targets to data centres and underwater internet cables in the region. The situation has grown more volatile with the escalation of the Saudi-Houthi conflict. The Yemeni rebel group, which now controls a large part of the country and Bab al-Mandeb, a critical chokepoint on the Red Sea, has repeatedlystruckkey Saudi installations. Against that backdrop, the visit by senior Saudi officials to Tehran stands out as a significant outreach at a time of profound tension between the two countries, with Saudi Arabia absorbing near-daily attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis. The kingdom was represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid — the brother and trusted envoy of the crown prince. His decision to travel to Iran under such conditions signalled that the Saudi leadership wants to avert another round of hostilities between the US, Israel and Iran, which could bring Iranian retaliatory strikes on American interests and installations in Saudi Arabia while the kingdom is still battling the Houthis. For Iran, the presence of senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan has been symbolically important: Iranian officials are eager to sideline the US from regional security and diplomatic arrangements. Iran’s president expressed hope that the talks could help consolidate “regional unity and cohesion”. For all the positivity, the central question remains whether the meeting could bridge the gap and help prevent a new round of US-Israeli aggression against Iran and, more importantly, de-escalate the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. No joint statement was issued, but individual comments since have been encouraging on the possibility of a broader regional security mechanism. Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, seemed satisfied after meeting officials from the three countries. “Very good discussions took place between us,” he told Iranian state television. “I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region. … I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen.” Iranian officials are also hopeful that the meeting could be a prelude to further steps towards shaping “endogenous security — an issue that we have been insisting on for decades”. The four countries have “agreed to continue discussions to strengthen cooperation … including on regional peace and security”. Indeed, the Tehran meeting was the most significant development yet that could help de-escalate the regional conflict. But the major question remains whether such emerging cooperation can prevent a fresh American-Israeli attack on Iran. The reported reinforcement of American forces in the region, together with Israel’s continued genocidal war in Gaza and military action in Lebanon, poses the biggest threat to regional and global peace. The continued presence of American bases and troops in the Gulf countries has made their security far more vulnerable. Most concerning is the escalating Saudi-Houthi conflict, which could trigger a wider conflagration and draw other countries into it. Iran could certainly play an important role in reaching a truce. The escalation could also hand Israel an opportunity to blunt resistance to its expansionist designs. Given Trump’s threatening rhetoric, there is a strong possibility that he will resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections; the one thing that could stop him is the Republicans losing their majority in both the House and the Senate. And whatever the outcome of the Israeli general elections, there is no indication that the defeat of Netanyahu would change the policy of the Zionist state in any significant way. The divisions among regional countries give Israel complete impunity. The quadrilateral meeting in Tehran and Iran’s positive response are certainly good omens. But the sources of tension remain that will not be easy to resolve, and the gap has yet to be bridged. It is vital that the Gulf countries refuse to let their soil be used for American aggression. Regional security can be ensured only through a regional security architecture. The Tehran meeting has provided an important opening for any such cooperation.
articles.author: Zahid Hussain

articles.title: Constitutional questions
articles.content: PAKISTAN has had three constitutions. Two given to it by its people in 1956 and 1973. One promulgated by a field marshal in 1962. The 1973 Constitution was adopted by the people through their representatives in the constituent assembly. Article 1 states that Pakistan shall be a federal republic. Neither the term “federal” nor “republic” is expressly defined. The Objectives Resolution provides guidance. The power and authority of the state in our republic is to be exercised through the chosen representatives of the people. A republic is distinct from rule by one man. In a republic, rulers are not immune from accountability. They can be removed and replaced if they fail to perform. The various territories that are part of Pakistan or that accede to Pakistan form a federation. These territories are autonomous and their boundaries and powers and authority are prescribed. The Objectives Resolution guarantees that the integrity of the territories shall be safeguarded. A federal state is brought into being by the territories that comprise it through a written instrument. This instrument defines the authority of the federation and these territories. The federation presupposes and is premised on the existence of these territories. Dismantling the territories would undermine the foundational integrity of the federation and the compact reflected in the 1973 Constitution. A constitution can be amended. The limits of a province or territory can be changed with its consent. Such an amendment may alter limits or provincial boundaries. It does not contemplate partition or subdivision of existing provinces or existing territories. Actions that compromise provincial integrity inevitably lead to questions regarding the benefits of being part of the federation. These questions have been resolved by the various territories and reflected in the 1973 Constitution. It would not be wise to reopen them. Emergency powers cannot be used to deprive any citizen of the right to a fair trial. Provincial integrity is not incompatible with devolution of power and effective local government. The Principles of Policy of the Constitution require the state to encourage local government institutions. Each province is constitutionally required to establish a local government system and to devolve power. The president is the head of state and represents the unity of the republic. The president as a symbol of a united federation must be satisfied prior to provincial autonomy being assailed. This can only be done in exceptional circumstances. The emergency provisions enable federal rule over a province if the president is satisfied that certain conditions exist. The president does not have authority to impose an emergency whenever he deems fit. The emergency provisions are not like the erstwhile Article 58(2)(b). The president was empowered under this Article to dissolve an elected government in his discretion. The emergency powers are not expressed to be discretionary powers of the president. Could the president have refused to sign therecent emergency proclamationnotwithstanding the advice of the federal government? He could certainly have asked the government to look at matters again. Did he have discretion to refuse if after reconsideration the government insisted? The term “discretion” is not used in the relevant Articles of the Constitution. The conventional legal view is that absent a power being expressed as discretionary, the president is bound to act on the advice of the government. In the case of the emergency provisions the president is required to be “satisfied”. This suggests a mental state of an individual office holder. It could be argued that a mental state cannot be imposed through governmental advice. Regardless, in the present emergency, this appears to be a moot point since the president did not even ask the government to reconsider its advice. We do not know the nature of the material made available to the president to satisfy him beyond what is contained in the proclamation. Its contents are in substance assertions and non-speaking. They do not provide cogent reasons. If the stipulated conditions for an emergency do not exist, the proclamation is unlawful. It is incorrect to state that because emergency powers exist in the Constitution, the exercise thereof is constitutional. The existence of a power and its lawful exercise are two distinct matters. Emergency powers cannot be used to deprive any citizen of Pakistan of the right to a fair trial. The emergency provisions enable suspension of operation of a provision of the Constitution only relating to a body or authority in the province. They do not permit the suspension of Article 10-A of the Constitution which provides for a fair trial and due process. The federal government’s order pursuant to the proclamation states that Article 175(3) shall not apply to the designated districts. This Article provides for separation of the judiciary from the executive. The constitutional framework does not contemplate such suspension. The emergency provisions also do not authorise the subdivision of a province by creating a separate governance structure for certain designated parts absent provincial legislative consent. Where certain federally administered areas have been made part of a province through a constitutional amendment (as is the case with Fata), the impact of this amendment cannot lawfully be undone through a proclamation of emergency which is an executive action. Depriving people of a territory of rule by their representatives is undemocratic and diminishes the federation. When imposed on an unwilling provincial government, it pits the centre against one of its parts and weakens the whole. Normal constitutional functioning should be restored as soon as possible. The real question that needs consideration is whether currently Pakistan is truly operating as a federal republic. That is what is contemplated by the first Article of our Constitution. If the compact that binds the territories that comprise our nation is broken, what credible vision can the rulers offer the people in these territories? The existential challenge the country faces is not from its enemies and those who wish us ill. It is from power being divorced from political authority and therefore accountability. That is the real emergency facing us. Until we confront this truth, the story of Pakistan will not change.
articles.author: Khwaja Ahmad Hosain

articles.title: Lula’s triumph
articles.content: LUIZ Inácio da Silva turned 81 yesterday with much more than a birthday to celebrate. Two days earlier, the man known as Lula pulled off a remarkable triumph, converting a deficit in the first round of Brazil’s presidential elections into a nearly 4m lead in the second round, thereby securing an unprecedented fourth term. The carnivalesque eruption of joy across much of Brazil was accompanied by an almost global sigh of relief. Flávio Bolsonaro’s first-round advantage compounded the fear of a candidate strongly favoured by the Trump and Netanyahu administrations pursuing his father’s fascistic agenda with even greater fervour. The would-be dynasty’s paterfamilias, Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for trying to instigate a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. On the eve of last Sunday’s vote, Reuters reported that US State Department officials had informed American diplomats in Brasilia that the aim was to restore Bolsonaro Sr to power. The extent to which that revelation might have fired up voters is open to conjecture, although previous attempts by Washington to rattle the Lula administration backfired, bolstering his popularity. More consequentially, the Lula campaign changed tack after the first round, shifting its focus from the Bolsonaro family’s crimes to direct action towards easing economic pressures. These included, belatedly, a five-day week, free weekend travel on public transport, more generous welfare payments, and a ban on online gambling. Such measures served as a reminder of Lula’s record since first winning the presidency in 2002 (following three failed attempts). Broadly speaking, he avoided challenging the precepts of neoliberalism, focusing instead on blunting the rougher edges of predatory capitalism, thereby lifting tens of millions out of poverty and reducing the historic economic and racial inequalities exacerbated by Brazil’s 21 years of military rule. As head of the metalworkers’ union from 1975, Lula’s militant activism was instrumental in challenging the dictatorship. Five years later, he helped found the Partido dos Trabalhadores, whose initial revolutionary zeal was replaced by social democratic ‘pragmatism’. The victory offers hope the far right can be thwarted electorally. During a 1984 visit to Britain, Lula said food and jobs were the primary need, rather than any dramatic upheaval. It took him 18 years to reach the presidency, during what was dubbed Latin America’s ‘pink tide’, spearheaded by Hugo Chavez in Venezuela under the fraternal (or perhaps paternal) gaze of Cuba’s Fidel Castro. Some on the left derided Lula’s incremental approach to redressing Brazil’s woes, but in retrospect it has arguably proved wiser than radical haste. Unlike most of his progressive contemporaries, Lula has survived to serve as a bulwark against the Trump administration’s imperialist designs, exemplified by seven consecutive electoral victories for the far right in Latin America. It has been a close call, though. Brazil’s size makes it easier to push back against hegemonic bullies. Sunday’s result can largely be accounted for by the Lula campaign’s bold strategy between the two electoral rounds, incorporating socioeconomic relief, impressive social media outreach that helped to sharply increase the turnout, and mass mobilisations by (mainly) young Brazilians appalled by the prospect of the Bolsonaros’ return. Lula will struggle to implement his agenda in the face of a hostile parliament, and a new, younger leadership must emerge to guide the Brazilian left’s fortunes. Yet the lesson that the designs of extreme right forces can electorally be thwarted despite the full-throated support of the US, Israel and the tech oligarchs will resonate far beyond Latin America — not least in Europe, where profoundly regressive forces are preparing to pounce as incumbent centrists struggle to offer any hope to disillusioned electorates. Long-time Serbian autocrat Aleksandar Vucic’s decisive defeat, also on Sunday, against a Student List thrown up by young protesters who have regularly been mobilising since a poorly constructed train station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad almost exactly two years ago, killing 16 people, sets another interesting example (not least for India’s inspiring agitators). They didn’t just march, they also organised at a grassroots level, and put up a list comprising a diverse range of academics and other professionals. Whether the victors will sensibly handle their surprising success remains to be seen, but it’s a hopeful trend. Equally unexpected was Vucic’s early concession speech, in contrast to Flávio Bolsonaro’s ridiculous diatribe against extended voting hours that his campaign had also sought. Not least for the sake of the Amazon rainforest, it must be hoped that the Bolsonaro project is dead. But, as Lula must know, complacency would be folly.
articles.author: Mahir Ali

articles.title: AI’s brain & muscle
articles.content: ARTIFICIAL intelligence is usually presented as weightless, almost entirely digital. We ask it to write, calculate, translate or create an image, and the response appears instantly. Yet every answer depends on a substantial physical system. This comprises data centres, specialised processors, cooling equipment etc. In reality AI has both ‘brain’ and ‘muscle’. Algorithms, software, researchers, engineers and companies comprise its brain. Its muscle consists of electricity, computing infrastructure, minerals, manufacturing capacity and reliable networks. The first phase of global AI competition focused mainly on the brain. As AI becomes more widely used, the muscle is becoming impossible to ignore. The International Energy Agency expects electricity demand from data centres to more than double by 2030, with AI a major driver. The challenge is not simply producing more power. It is producing reliable electricity supply and expanded transmission networks to accommodate the needs of large data centres. Oil and gas reserves beneath the ground are not the same as electricity delivered to a data centre. Resources become strategic only when they can be converted into dependable infrastructure. The physical foundations of AI also include copper, aluminium, silicon, and rare-earth materials. Advanced semiconductor technologies depend on specialised materials, while mining and refining remain concentrated in a limited number of countries. The digital economy has not escaped geography! An algorithm can cross a border in milliseconds, but a power plant, mine or factory cannot. This creates a new geopolitical equation. Countries with the strongest AI research and software ecosystems may still depend on others for energy, minerals and manufacturing. Resource-rich countries, meanwhile, may possess the muscle of the AI economy without the universities, capital, software and semiconductor capabilities needed to turn it into computing power. The long-term advantage may belong to countries that can connect the two. The digital economy has not escaped geography. Pakistan illustrates this challenge clearly. It is not currently a leading frontier-AI power and faces serious constraints in reliable electricity, advanced computing, research funding etc. Yet it has a large young population, growing software and IT-services sectors, universities, engineering talent, hydropower and renewable-energy potential, and significant mineral resources. The strategic challenge is therefore not simply to acquire more resources or develop more algorithms, but to connect the country’s physical assets with its scientific and technological capabilities. That would require moving beyond traditional models of exporting raw materials and low-value services. An AI-era strategy would use reliable energy, connectivity and mineral resources to support data centres, cloud services, local research, advanced applications and value-added manufacturing. AI could strengthen sectors such as agriculture, textiles, logistics, mining, health, education and public administration. In this model, AI becomes an industrial multiplier rather than merely another software sector. Resource wealth alone, however, guarantees neither technological independence nor prosperity. Natural resources cannot substitute for universities, skilled workers, capital, innovation and capable institutions. The relationship between AI’s brain and muscle is better understood as multiplication rather than addition. A country with excellent algorithms but unreliable power will struggle to scale, while a country with abundant energy but weak research capacity may remain a commodity supplier. The lesson extends beyond Pakistan. Countries such as the United States have extraordinary strengths in research, capital, technology companies and advanced computing. China combines rapidly advancing AI with industrial scale and manufacturing capacity. Gulf countries possess energy and capital, while Australia and Canada have substantial mineral and energy advantages. None controls every part of the AI system. Interdependence will remain unavoidable, but countries that connect more stages, from energy and minerals to computing and applications, will have greater strategic influence. For Pakistan and other natural resource-rich countries, the message is immediate. An AI strategy cannot stop at applications, start-ups or policy statements. It must also address reliable electricity, data-centre infrastructure, digital skills, research institutions, mineral value addition and industrial capacity. The next phase of the AI race will not be decided solely by who builds the smartest models. It will also be decided by who can power them, supply them and apply them productively. AI has a brain. But without muscle, even the most brilliant brain cannot move.
articles.author: Nazir A. Jogezai

articles.title: Regional security
articles.content: THE fact that high officials from the Makkah defence pact partner states — Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye —were in Tehranon Monday made global headlines, and with good reason. At a time when the clouds of war are once again hovering over the Gulf, the meeting sent a strong message that regional states with often competing agendas can come together and discuss their issues at the negotiating table. The event was also significant as the Makkah alliance has been seen as an alternative defence arrangement vis-à-vis Iran’s ‘Axis of Resistance’. Pakistan was represented by the chief of defence forces, while significantly, Saudi Arabia sent its defence minister, a brother of the crown prince. This shows that Riyadh accorded the highest priority to the meeting. The official Iranian readout said the participants pledged to “continue the dialogue … for peace and security in the region.” The event is also further proof of Pakistan’s constructive efforts in the diplomatic arena, as the meet-up was held after the CDF — who was in Tehran last week — suggested it. All regional states are wary of possible fresh US/Israeli attacks on Iran, and the Tehran meeting must be seen in this framework. Moreover, Saudi Arabia has likely reached out to Iran to get the Islamic Republic to use its connections with Yemen’s Houthi Ansarallah group to stop its attacks on the kingdom. Riyadh is also concerned about Iranian retaliation in the face of a renewed Israeli and American attack. Perhaps Yemen can be the first area for the Makkah pact allies and Iran to discuss. A fresh push for peace should be made that envisages an immediate ceasefire supplemented by an end to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, and a lifting of the Saudi-led blockade on Houthi-held areas in Yemen. Both Saudi Arabia and Iran, as well as other regional powers, should advocate a negotiated settlement to the Yemeni civil war. Beyond Yemen, the fact that the US and Israel are preparing for fresh aggression against Iran could spoil efforts for a regional entente. This is why all participants of the Tehran meeting must clearly say that they oppose attacks on Iran or any other regional state. Iran and the Makkah pact states should also pledge not to let external actors use their soil to launch aggression against each other. In fact, while inviting Iran to join the Makkah alliance may not be practical at this juncture, regional states can at least agree to a common non-aggression framework. That would send a powerful message to external actors that seek to destabilise the region. States of the region are making sincere efforts to prevent a return to war. It is time Washington and Tel Aviv read the writing on the wall and abandoned their destructive plans.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Rate hike
articles.content: THE SBP’s decision to raise its policy rate by 50 basis points to 12pc was largely expected. It is also justified by growing risks to price stability. Although the increase has disappointed many businesses seeking cheaper credit, the monetary policy cannot be determined by their immediate financing needs. With global inflation proving stickier than expected, borrowing costs remaining high internationally, and domestic energy prices vulnerable to fresh external shocks, cutting or holding rates was no option. Pakistan’s recent currency stability, rising reserves and strong remittances have strengthened its external position. Still, these gains do not insulate the economy from the shocks of the Gulf war, or from tighter global financial conditions. Competition for capital is intensifying as major central banks tighten monetary policy, while the IMF expects global inflation to reach 4.7pc. In this environment, the SBP must guard against entrenched inflation expectations and potential pressure on the rupee. Currency stability, achieved partly through subdued imports, cannot be treated as evidence that external vulnerabilities have disappeared. An abrupt increase in import demand, a rise in energy prices or tighter global financial conditions could quickly expose those weaknesses. The hike is a precaution against losing the gains made so far. Foreign investors have welcomed the hike, viewing it as necessary to contain inflation and safeguard macroeconomic stability amid global energy risks. However, trade bodies argue that inflation is driven by supply constraints, energy costs and fiscal distortions rather than excessive demand. Industry associations have similarly warned that expensive credit could force already struggling factories to cut production or shelve expansion plans. These concerns are legitimate. Industrial recovery remains fragile, and an extended period of expensive financing could weaken investment, employment and exports. But the answer is not to dismiss monetary tightening simply because it imposes costs. Tight money is no cure for supply-side inflationary pressures. But it keeps hard-won stability from slipping by anchoring expectations and protecting the rupee. The real relief for industry must come from lasting tax, power and regulatory reforms.
articles.author: Editorial
